newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Ex-Fed officials see no Nov 13 tightening.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Ex-Fed officials see no Nov 13 tightening.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Board will likely remove its current bias toward tighter credit at the November 13 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, former Fed officials said.
They also said they expect the central bank to keep monetary policy steady. Separately, a Reuters survey showed 37 economists at primary dealers see interest rates unchanged as well.
The Fed adopted a tightening bias in July after a string of economic data depicted a robust U.S. economy.
But the current state of the economy has all the trappings to cause the central bank to exchange its tightening bias for a symmetric directive, the former Fed officials said.
"The economy is one in which a likelihood of easing and a likelihood of tightening are not greatly different," said former Fed Governor Lyle Gramley.
Gramley noted Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in the third quarter showed very weak personal consumption expenditures but strong inventory investment.
According to the Commerce Department's advance estimate, GDP grew at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter, down from 4.7 percent in the second quarter.
"So the logical thing (for the Fed) to do would be to adopt a symmetric directive (to neutrality)," Gramley said.
Preston Martin, former vice chairman of the Fed board, concurred.

Martin said the Fed's latest Beige Book report on regional business conditions, covering the end of September and most of October, might have quieted any regional bank presidents who had called for tighter policy.
"I think they will be less assertive with regard to the need for steps to avert inflation," said Martin, the chairman of HomeVest Financial Services Inc.
"The Beige Book reads better this time than the previous time," he added.
The former fed officials added they believe recent economic data suggest inflation has waned and the economy is sluggishly moving forward.
But their views on how and when the Fed will respond differ.
Philip Jackson, a former Fed Governor, said he expects the fourth quarter to be slower than the third.

"People are not buying things," said Jackson who is a finance professor at Birmingham Southern College in Birmingham, Ala. Since the Fed operates on "anecdotal evidence," there is no reason for the central bank to tighten monetary policy at the meeting, he said.
But Gramley, a consulting economist for the Mortgage Bankers Association, said increasing price pressures might induce the Fed to rein in credit sometime during the first quarter of 1997.
"This economy is clearly not moving, but it's in fundamentally quite good condition," he said.

Noting the unemployment rate, now at 5.2 percent, Gramley said it is "about as low as it can go without generating inflationary pressures." Gramley said if business fixed investment generated economic growth above the long-term growth potential (about 2.5 percent), that would mean further declines in unemployment and eventually, a rise in inflation.
William Ford, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, said a first quarter rate hike is possible but unlikely.

"If the economy's growth rate were to accelerate, and if that would create higher demand for jobs, we could see some wage pressure which would lead to cost-push inflation -- which the Fed might respond to," said Ford, an economics and finance professor at Middle Tennessee state University.
"But I don't see it by the end of this month or the end of the year," added Ford.
